newsitem.title: USA: Weekly jobless claims up in latest week.
newsitem.headline: Weekly jobless claims up in latest week.

text.p: The number of Americans lining up to collect first-time unemployment benefits rose by 5,000 last week, the government said Thursday, but analysts said the level of new claims still suggested a strengthening economy.

The Labour Department said weekly jobless claims rose to 322,000 in the week ended May 17 from a downwardly revised 317,000 the week earlier. The new claims activity fell short of Wall Street's forecast of 324,000 claims.

The four-week moving average climbed to 333,250 from a revised 332,500 a week earlier. Economists usually view the average as a more reliable yardstick of jobless trends because it evens out weekly fluctuations in the data.
But automobile industry strikes and Midwestern flooding have skewed the moving average recently, making it a less useful gauge for now, some economists said.
New applications for jobless benefits had jumped significantly a few weeks earlier as the impact of the auto strikes and the flooding filtered through to workers.

Those special factors had interrupted a downward trend in new claims filings, which appear to be returning to levels seen in January and February, when employment was growing at its strongest pace this year, economists said.

"That clearly is not acceptable to financial markets and policy makers," said Anthony Chan, chief economist at Banc One Investment Advisors Corp. in Columbus, Ohio. "It really is suggestive of a labour market that continues to be very firm."
Economists also said they would not be surprised to see jobs being created at a faster pace in May than in recent months.
"I wouldn't cheer if I were looking for a slowing economy," said Tim O'Neill, chief economist at Harris Bank/Bank of Montreal. "This is an economy that's going to bounce again."
The Federal Reserve decided on Tuesday to leave interest rates unchanged in hopes that economic growth would slow on its own from its recent pace.

The total number of Americans continuing to claim unemployment benefits rose in the week ended May 10, the latest period for which that data were available. That figure swelled to 2,299,000 from 2,289,000 the week before.
The department said nine states reported decreases in claims exceeding 1,000 on an unadjusted basis in the week ended May 10, the latest period for which that data were available.
Among the largest were New York with 6,336 fewer jobless claims, North Dakota with 2,231, Minnesota with 1,841, Kentucky with 1,758 and New Jersey with 1,399.

Despite the drop in North Dakota's claims activity, claims in that state were still higher than normal due to flooding, the department said. In Minnesota, more than 700 claims were reported as flood-related.

Kentucky reported fewer layoffs in the rubber industry, while New Jersey said it had fewer layoffs in the transportation, trade and service industries and in manufacturing. New York provided no comment.

The department said four states reported increases in claims exceeding 1,000, unadjusted, in the May 10 week. They were Pennsylvania with 1,582 additional filings, Tennessee with 1,452, Ohio with 1,064 and Alabama with 1,011.
Pennsylvania reported layoffs in the trade, service, chemical and fabricated metals industries.

Tennessee said it had layoffs in the construction, service, food, apparel, and electronic equipment industries, and in manufacturing. Alabama reported layoffs in the textile and electrical machinery industries. Ohio gave no explanation.
